      "body": "# Matching Market (One-to-One)\n\nA **one-to-one matching market** consists of:\n\n- A finite nonempty set $M$ of *men* (proposers).\n- A finite nonempty set $W$ of *women* (receivers).\n- For each $i \\in M$, a strict linear order $\\succ_i$ over $W \\cup \\{\\bot_i\\}$,\n  where $\\bot_i$ represents staying unmatched.\n- For each $j \\in W$, a strict linear order $\\succ_j$ over $M \\cup \\{\\bot_j\\}$.\n\nWe say $j$ is **acceptable** to $i$ if $j \\succ_i \\bot_i$ (and symmetrically for\n$i$ acceptable to $j$). The market makes no use of cardinal utilities — only\nthe ordinal preferences matter.\n\nIn Lean this is the `MatchingMarket` structure under\n`EconCSLib.MarketDesign.Matching.Basic`. The \"two-sided\" terminology refers to\nthe two disjoint participant sets $M$, $W$; \"one-to-one\" refers to each\nparticipant being matched to at most one partner.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.22, Def 22.1] Maschler, Solan, Zamir, *Game Theory*."

      "body": "# Matching (Partial Bijection)\n\nGiven a one-to-one matching market $(M, W, \\succ)$, a **matching** is a\npartial function $\\mu : M \\to W \\cup \\{\\bot\\}$ together with the dual\n$\\mu^{-1} : W \\to M \\cup \\{\\bot\\}$ such that:\n\n- $\\mu$ is injective on its matched domain (a man is matched to at most one woman).\n- $\\mu(i) = j \\iff \\mu^{-1}(j) = i$ for $i \\in M$, $j \\in W$ (consistency).\n- If $\\mu(i) = \\bot$ we say $i$ is **unmatched**; symmetric for $j$.\n\nEquivalently, $\\mu$ is a set $\\{(i, j) : \\mu(i) = j\\} \\subseteq M \\times W$ in\nwhich each element of $M$ appears at most once and each element of $W$ appears\nat most once.\n\nIn Lean this corresponds to the `Matching M W` structure in\n`EconCSLib.MarketDesign.Matching.Basic` carrying both sides of the partial\nbijection plus the consistency invariant.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.22, Def 22.2] Maschler, Solan, Zamir, *Game Theory*."

      "body": "# Gale-Shapley Theorem\n\n**Theorem.** Every finite one-to-one matching market $(M, W, \\succ)$ admits\na stable matching. Specifically, the matching output by the men-proposing\ndeferred-acceptance algorithm ([[gale_shapley_algorithm]]) is stable.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nRun the men-proposing algorithm to completion (termination is guaranteed by\nthe proposal-count argument).\n\nLet $\\mu$ be the output matching. We verify the two stability conditions:\n\n**Individual rationality.** A man $i$ only ever proposes to women he finds\nacceptable (the algorithm consults his preference list). A woman $j$ only\never holds offers from men she finds acceptable (she rejects unacceptable\nproposers). Hence every matched pair is mutually acceptable.\n\n**No blocking pair.** Suppose toward contradiction that $(i, j)$ blocks\n$\\mu$, i.e., $j \\succ_i \\mu(i)$ and $i \\succ_j \\mu^{-1}(j)$.\n\nSince $j \\succ_i \\mu(i)$, woman $j$ ranks higher than $\\mu(i)$ on man $i$'s\nlist, so $i$ must have proposed to $j$ at some round (before settling for\n$\\mu(i)$ or staying unmatched). At the round $i$ proposed to $j$:\n\n- Either $j$ rejected $i$, in which case $j$ was holding (or later switched\n  to) some man $i'$ with $i' \\succ_j i$, OR\n- $j$ accepted $i$ but was later replaced by some $i' \\succ_j i$.\n\nIn either case, once $j$ has held an offer she never reverts to unmatched\nand her holding partner only ever improves (the algorithm has \"no-going-back\"\nmonotonicity on the receiving side). So her final partner satisfies\n$\\mu^{-1}(j) \\succeq_j i'$ for the rejecting/replacing $i'$, and since\n$i' \\succ_j i$ we get $\\mu^{-1}(j) \\succ_j i$ — contradicting\n$i \\succ_j \\mu^{-1}(j)$.\n\n## Lean Status\n\n**Proved** (no `sorry`) at\n`EconCSLib.MarketDesign.Matching.GaleShapley.galeShapley_isStable`; axiom scan\nshows only `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`. Closed under MT-L1\n(#203). The two structural ingredients are now in place:\n\n1. The \"monotone holding\" invariant `holding_rank_mono_run` (+ the\n   stay-matched companion `held_preserved_run`): a woman's holding partner\n   can only improve over time and she never reverts to unmatched.\n2. The \"no free men at termination\" property `finalState_no_free_men`,\n   from the cursor-sum growth bound versus the `n*n` proposal ceiling.\n\nThe blocking-pair argument is assembled in the `RSInv` (Roth–Sotomayor)\nrun-state invariant and discharged by `rsinv_stability`.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.22, Thm 22.7] Maschler, Solan, Zamir, *Game Theory*.\n- Gale & Shapley (1962)."

      "body": "# Proposing-Side Optimal Stable Matching\n\n**Theorem.** Let $\\mu^M$ denote the matching produced by the men-proposing\nGale-Shapley algorithm on $(M, W, \\succ)$. Then:\n\n1. **Men-optimal.** For every man $i \\in M$ and every stable matching $\\mu$:\n\n   $$\\mu^M(i) \\succeq_i \\mu(i)$$\n\n   I.e., every man weakly prefers his match in $\\mu^M$ to his match in any\n   other stable matching.\n\n2. **Women-pessimal.** For every woman $j \\in W$ and every stable matching $\\mu$:\n\n   $$\\mu(j) \\succeq_j \\mu^M(j)$$\n\n   I.e., every woman weakly prefers her match in any other stable matching\n   to her match in $\\mu^M$.\n\nA symmetric pair of statements holds for the women-proposing algorithm with\nroles swapped.\n\n## Conventions\n\n- Write $\\mu(a)$ for the partner of agent $a$ under matching $\\mu$, in either\n  direction; the matching bijection gives $\\mu(i) = j \\iff \\mu(j) = i$.\n- Preferences are **strict**: each agent's preference list is a full ranking\n  with no ties (the standard marriage-market setting). Strictness is used in\n  the women-pessimal part.\n- The men-proposing algorithm has each man propose down his list in\n  **decreasing order of preference**, advancing past any woman who rejects\n  him or who later displaces him.\n- The market is **balanced** ($|M| = |W|$) with full preference lists, so the\n  men-proposing algorithm terminates with a **perfect matching** — every agent\n  is matched. This is the termination half of the [[gale_shapley_stable]]\n  existence result this node builds on, and is what lets the conclusion below\n  speak of *the* partner $\\mu^M(i)$ of each man.\n\n## Proof\n\nCall a man-woman pair $(i, j)$ **achievable** if some stable matching matches\n$i$ to $j$.\n\n### Men-optimal\n\nWe prove the invariant: **throughout the men-proposing algorithm, no man is\never rejected by an achievable partner**, where \"rejected\" covers both a fresh\nproposal turned away and a tentatively-held man later displaced.\n\n*Base case.* Before any proposals are made no rejection has occurred, so the\ninvariant holds vacuously.\n\n*Inductive step.* Assume the invariant holds up to the current round, and for\ncontradiction suppose man $i$ is rejected by an achievable partner $j$ in this\nround. Pick a stable matching $\\mu$ with $\\mu(i) = j$. When $j$ rejects $i$ she\nis holding some man $i'$ with $i' \\succ_j i$.\n\nWe show $i'$ strictly prefers $j$ to his $\\mu$-partner $\\mu(i')$:\n\n- $(i', \\mu(i'))$ is achievable (witnessed by $\\mu$), so by the inductive\n  hypothesis $i'$ has **not** been rejected by $\\mu(i')$ up to this round.\n- $j \\neq \\mu(i')$: otherwise $\\mu$ would match both $i$ and $i'$ to $j$, which\n  is impossible for a one-to-one matching (note $i' \\neq i$ since\n  $i' \\succ_j i$).\n- Hence $i'$ has not yet **proposed** to $\\mu(i')$. For if he had proposed and\n  (by the IH) not been rejected, the invariant would force $i'$ to be holding\n  $\\mu(i')$ right now — but he is holding $j \\neq \\mu(i')$.\n- Yet $i'$ *has* proposed to $j$ (he is holding her). Since men propose in\n  decreasing order of preference, every woman $i'$ has not yet proposed to —\n  in particular $\\mu(i')$ — is strictly below $j$ in his ranking:\n  $j \\succ_{i'} \\mu(i')$.\n\nSo $(i', j)$ is a blocking pair for $\\mu$: $i' \\succ_j i = \\mu(j)$ on the woman\nside, and $j \\succ_{i'} \\mu(i')$ on the man side. This contradicts the\nstability of $\\mu$. Therefore $j$ is not achievable for $i$, establishing the\ninvariant.\n\n*Conclusion.* At termination man $i$ is held by some woman $\\mu^M(i)$ (his last\nand most recent successful proposal). Let $j$ be any achievable partner of\n$i$. By the invariant $i$ was not rejected by $j$, so either $j = \\mu^M(i)$, or\n$i$ never proposed to $j$. In the latter case $j$ lies strictly below\n$\\mu^M(i)$ in $i$'s ranking (he proposed exactly to the prefix of his list up\nto $\\mu^M(i)$), so $\\mu^M(i) \\succ_i j$. Either way $\\mu^M(i) \\succeq_i j$.\nTaking $j = \\mu(i)$ for an arbitrary stable matching $\\mu$ — achievable by\ndefinition — yields the men-optimal statement.\n\n### Women-pessimal\n\nFix a stable matching $\\mu$ and a woman $j$; set $i = \\mu^M(j)$ and\n$i' = \\mu(j)$. Suppose for contradiction that $j$ is strictly better off under\n$\\mu^M$, i.e. $i \\succ_j i'$.\n\nApplying the men-optimal statement to man $i$ (whose $\\mu^M$-partner is $j$) gives\n$j = \\mu^M(i) \\succeq_i \\mu(i)$. Moreover $\\mu(i) \\neq j$ — otherwise\n$\\mu(j) = i = i'$ would make $i \\succ_j i'$ read $i \\succ_j i$, false — so by\nstrictness of preferences the comparison is strict: $j \\succ_i \\mu(i)$.\n\nThen $(i, j)$ blocks $\\mu$: $i \\succ_j i' = \\mu(j)$ on the woman side and\n$j \\succ_i \\mu(i)$ on the man side, contradicting stability. Hence no woman is\nstrictly better off under $\\mu^M$; that is, $\\mu(j) \\succeq_j \\mu^M(j)$.\n\n## Consequences\n\nThe set of stable matchings has a **distinguished extremal element** on each\nside. Combined with the [[lattice]] structure, this gives an explicit\ncharacterization of the boundary of the stable set.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.22, Thm 22.11] Maschler, Solan, Zamir, *Game Theory*.\n- Gale & Shapley (1962), original optimality observation.\n- Roth & Sotomayor (1990), *Two-Sided Matching*, Ch. 2."

The join $\\mu \\vee \\mu'$ matches each\nman to his preferred of the two partners; the meet $\\mu \\wedge \\mu'$ matches\neach man to his less-preferred. Both are stable matchings.\n\nEquivalently, under $\\le_W$ defined dually (women's preference), the lattice\nis the order-dual.\n\n## Extrema\n\n- Top under $\\le_M$: the **men-optimal** matching $\\mu^M$ (output of\n  men-proposing GS — see [[proposing_optimal]]).\n- Bottom under $\\le_M$: the **women-optimal** matching $\\mu^W$ (output of\n  women-proposing GS).\n\nThese two are also the bottom and top respectively under $\\le_W$ — the men's\nand women's interests are exactly opposed across the stable set.\n\n## Proof Sketch\n\nThe non-trivial part is showing $\\mu \\vee \\mu'$ (each man picks his preferred\npartner from $\\mu$ and $\\mu'$) is itself a matching (not just a function) and\nis stable.\n\n*Matching*: We must show no woman is \"picked\" by two different men.       "body": "# Rural Hospitals Theorem\n\n**Theorem (Roth 1986; McVitie–Wilson 1970 for one-to-one).** In a finite\none-to-one matching market $(M, W, \\succ)$, the set of **matched participants**\nis invariant across all stable matchings:\n\n$$\\{ i \\in M : \\mu(i) \\ne \\bot \\} = \\{ i \\in M : \\mu'(i) \\ne \\bot \\}$$\n\nfor any two stable matchings $\\mu, \\mu'$ (and symmetrically for $W$). In\nparticular the man-optimal $\\mu^M$ and woman-optimal $\\mu^W$ match exactly the\nsame individuals.\n\n## Formalized specialization: balanced full-preference markets\n\nThe Lean model (`Preferences n` via `MatchingMarket.ofEquivData`) is the\n**balanced full-preference** case: $|M| = |W| = n$ and every agent ranks every\nagent on the other side (no $\\bot$). There the theorem sharpens to:\n\n> **Every stable matching is perfect** — all $n$ men and all $n$ women are\n> matched.\n\nSo the matched set is all of $\\mathrm{Fin}\\,n$ in *every* stable matching and\ninvariance is immediate. This is `GS.stable_matching_perfect`.\n\n### Proof (balanced case)\n\nSuppose a woman $i_0$ is unmatched in a stable $\\mu$. If *every* man were\nmatched, then $\\mathrm{matchW} : \\text{men} \\to \\text{women}$ would be a total\ninjection on the finite equal-size set $\\mathrm{Fin}\\,n$, hence a bijection,\nmaking $i_0$ some man's partner — contradiction. So some man $j_0$ is also\nunmatched. But then $(i_0, j_0)$ blocks $\\mu$: each strictly prefers *any*\npartner to staying single (since $\\bot$ is least-preferred), contradicting\nstability. The men side is symmetric, using totality of $\\mathrm{matchM}$.\n\nNo lattice machinery is needed in the balanced case — the argument is a direct\nfiniteness-plus-blocking-pair contradiction.\n\n## General case (⊥ and unequal sets)\n\nWith unacceptable partners or $|M| \\ne |W|$, stable matchings genuinely *can*\nleave agents unmatched, and the theorem becomes the non-trivial invariance\nstatement above. The standard proof routes through the [[lattice]] structure\n(WLOG compare $\\mu^M$ and $\\mu^W$). Formalizing this general version requires\nthe $\\bot$/acceptability extension of the Lean model and is tracked as future\nwork (#231 item D).\n\n## Why \"Rural Hospitals\"?\n\nThe name comes from the many-to-one (residency matching) version: any hospital\nthat fills fewer positions than its quota under one stable assignment fills\nexactly the same set of positions — with the same residents — under every\nstable assignment. Rural hospitals that struggle to fill positions still\nstruggle; no stable mechanism can rescue them within the stable-matching\nframework. The one-to-one statement above is the simplest specialization.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.22, Thm 22.14] Maschler, Solan, Zamir, *Game Theory*.\n- McVitie & Wilson (1970), *Stable Marriage Assignment for Unequal Sets*.\n- Roth (1986), *On the Allocation of Residents to Rural Hospitals*. Econometrica 54.\n- Roth & Sotomayor (1990), Ch. 2 §2.4."

      "body": "# Stability of a Matching\n\nLet $\\mu$ be a matching in a one-to-one matching market $(M, W, \\succ)$.\n\n## Individual Rationality\n\n$\\mu$ is **individually rational** if no participant is matched to an\nunacceptable partner:\n\n- For every $i \\in M$: $\\mu(i) = \\bot$ or $\\mu(i) \\succ_i \\bot_i$.\n- For every $j \\in W$: $\\mu^{-1}(j) = \\bot$ or $\\mu^{-1}(j) \\succ_j \\bot_j$.\n\n## Blocking Pair\n\nA pair $(i, j) \\in M \\times W$ **blocks** $\\mu$ if both members strictly\nprefer each other to their current $\\mu$-partner (treating $\\bot$ as the\nlowest-ranked alternative):\n\n- $j \\succ_i \\mu(i)$ (man $i$ prefers $j$ to his current match), AND\n- $i \\succ_j \\mu^{-1}(j)$ (woman $j$ prefers $i$ to her current match).\n\n## Stability\n\n$\\mu$ is **stable** if it is individually rational and admits no blocking pair.\n\nEquivalently, $\\mu$ is stable iff no pair $(i, j)$ would defect by mutually\nbreaking their current commitments and matching with each other.\n\nIn Lean, the three predicates live in `EconCSLib.MarketDesign.Matching.Basic`\nas `Matching.IsIndividuallyRational`, `Matching.IsBlocking`, and\n`Matching.IsStable`.\n\n## References\n\n- [MSZ Ch.22, Defs 22.3–22.5] Maschler, Solan, Zamir, *Game Theory*."

      "body": "# Gale-Shapley Deferred Acceptance Algorithm\n\nMen-proposing version on a one-to-one matching market $(M, W, \\succ)$.\n\n## Algorithm\n\nInitialize: every man is free; every woman holds no offer.\n\nRepeat until no free man has any acceptable woman remaining on his list:\n\n1. **Propose.** Pick a free man $i$ who still has at least one acceptable\n   woman not yet proposed to.         "body": "# Lattice of Stable Matchings

**Theorem (Conway, reported by Knuth 1976).** The set of stable matchings
of any finite one-to-one matching market forms a **complete distributive
lattice** under the partial order

$$\mu \le_M \mu' \quad \iff \quad \mu(i) \preceq_i \mu'(i) \text{ for all } i \in M$$

("men weakly prefer $\mu'$ to $\mu$"). The join $\mu \vee \mu'$ matches each
man to his preferred of the two partners; the meet $\mu \wedge \mu'$ matches
each man to his less-preferred. Both are stable matchings.

Equivalently, under $\le_W$ defined dually (women's preference), the lattice
is the order-dual.

## Extrema

- Top under $\le_M$: the **men-optimal** matching $\mu^M$ (output of
  men-proposing GS — see [[proposing_optimal]]).
- Bottom under $\le_M$: the **women-optimal** matching $\mu^W$ (output of
  women-proposing GS).

These two are also the bottom and top respectively under $\le_W$ — the men's
and women's interests are exactly opposed across the stable set.

## Proof Sketch

The non-trivial part is showing $\mu \vee \mu'$ (each man picks his preferred
partner from $\mu$ and $\mu'$) is itself a matching (not just a function) and
is stable.

*Matching*: We must show no woman is "picked" by two different men. If man
$i_1$'s preferred partner is $j$, and $i_2$'s preferred is also $j$, then $j$
is matched to $i_1$ in one of $\mu, \mu'$ and to $i_2$ in the other. By the
opposed-preferences phenomenon (a corollary of stability), $j$ also prefers
exactly the opposite — contradiction.

*Stability*: If $(i, k)$ blocks $\mu \vee \mu'$, then $k$ ranks higher on
$i$'s list than his max of $\mu(i), \mu'(i)$, so $(i, k)$ blocks both $\mu$
and $\mu'$ — contradicting stability of either.

Distributivity follows from the same opposed-preferences structure.

## Formalization

In the balanced full-preference Lean model (`Preferences n` via
`MatchingMarket.ofEquivData`, every stable matching perfect), the lattice
structure is formalized as a `Lattice` instance on
`GS.StableMatching w m` (`EconCSLib.MarketDesign.Matching.Lattice`):

- `GS.opposed_preferences` (+ `opposed_preferences_women`) — the
  opposed-preferences lemma, proved by a direct pairwise blocking argument.
- `GS.stableJoin` / `GS.stableMeet` — the join and meet as `Matching`s, each
  built from an injective-hence-bijective partner map (`joinWoman` /
  `meetMan`); the injectivity is the "no woman picked twice" step and uses
  `opposed_preferences`.
- `GS.stableJoin_isStable` / `GS.stableMeet_isStable` — both operations are
  closed within the stable set.
- The `Lattice (GS.StableMatching w m)` instance — the men-preference order
  (`σ ≤ τ` iff every man weakly prefers `τ`) with `⊔ = stableJoin`,
  `⊓ = stableMeet`, all lattice axioms discharged.
- `GS.StableMatching.gsStable_isGreatest` — the **men-proposing GS output is
  the greatest element** ($\top$) of this lattice: every man weakly prefers
  it to his partner in any other stable matching. This is
  [[proposing_optimal]] (`galeShapley_isProposingOptimal`) packaged as the
  lattice maximum, identifying the men-optimal extremum $\mu^M$ with the GS
  output.

All sorry-free (axioms: `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`).

**Not yet formalized** (classical, future refinements): *distributivity* of
the lattice, *completeness*, and the *women-proposing* bottom extremum
$\mu^W$ (no women-proposing GS is formalized yet). The general
$\bot$/unequal-cardinality version is also out of scope of the balanced model.

## Consequences

- The number of stable matchings is bounded by combinatorial counts on the
  lattice (e.g., chain lengths, antichains).
- The Conway-Knuth lattice is the foundation for the [[rural_hospitals]]
  invariant ("same set of matched participants across all stable matchings").

## References

- Knuth (1976), *Marriages Stables*. Université de Montréal.
- Roth & Sotomayor (1990), Ch. 2 §2.3."

**Theorem (Conway, reported by Knuth 1976).** The set of stable matchings
of any finite one-to-one matching market forms a **complete distributive
lattice** under the partial order

$$\mu \le_M \mu' \quad \iff \quad \mu(i) \preceq_i \mu'(i) \text{ for all } i \in M$$

("men weakly prefer $\mu'$ to $\mu$"). The join $\mu \vee \mu'$ matches each
man to his preferred of the two partners; the meet $\mu \wedge \mu'$ matches
each man to his less-preferred. Both are stable matchings.

Equivalently, under $\le_W$ defined dually (women's preference), the lattice
is the order-dual.

## Extrema

- Top under $\le_M$: the **men-optimal** matching $\mu^M$ (output of
  men-proposing GS — see [[proposing_optimal]]).
- Bottom under $\le_M$: the **women-optimal** matching $\mu^W$ (output of
  women-proposing GS).

These two are also the bottom and top respectively under $\le_W$ — the men's
and women's interests are exactly opposed across the stable set.

## Proof Sketch

The non-trivial part is showing $\mu \vee \mu'$ (each man picks his preferred
partner from $\mu$ and $\mu'$) is itself a matching (not just a function) and
is stable.

*Matching*: We must show no woman is "picked" by two different men. If man
$i_1$'s preferred partner is $j$, and $i_2$'s preferred is also $j$, then $j$
is matched to $i_1$ in one of $\mu, \mu'$ and to $i_2$ in the other. By the
opposed-preferences phenomenon (a corollary of stability), $j$ also prefers
exactly the opposite — contradiction.

*Stability*: If $(i, k)$ blocks $\mu \vee \mu'$, then $k$ ranks higher on
$i$'s list than his max of $\mu(i), \mu'(i)$, so $(i, k)$ blocks both $\mu$
and $\mu'$ — contradicting stability of either.

Distributivity follows from the same opposed-preferences structure.

## Formalization

In the balanced full-preference Lean model (`Preferences n` via
`MatchingMarket.ofEquivData`, every stable matching perfect), the lattice
structure is formalized as a `Lattice` instance on
`GS.StableMatching w m` (`EconCSLib.MarketDesign.Matching.Lattice`):

- `GS.opposed_preferences` (+ `opposed_preferences_women`) — the
  opposed-preferences lemma, proved by a direct pairwise blocking argument.
- `GS.stableJoin` / `GS.stableMeet` — the join and meet as `Matching`s, each
  built from an injective-hence-bijective partner map (`joinWoman` /

  `opposed_preferences`.
